name: Framing Effect
description: Equivalent options can lead to different choices depending on how they are described—for example as gains versus losses—even when the underlying outcomes are unchanged. Presentation changes judgment, not just cosmetics.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to pricing copy, consent language, risk communication, benefit-vs.-loss messaging, retention nudges, and any choice architecture that can be expressed in more than one equivalent way.
prevalence_note: A core prospect-theory idea, widely taught in behavioral design, policy, product messaging, and risk-communication practice.

findings.description: Many Labs 2's battery of 28 direct replications included Tversky & Kahneman's gain/loss framing effect (the 'Asian disease' paradigm already documented in this corpus as find-tversky-framing) as one of the tested effects, run across the study's 36-country, 125-sample design. Consistent with the study's aggregate pattern, the framing effect replicated in the same direction as the original demonstration but at a reduced magnitude relative to Tversky & Kahneman's original effect size; the study's exploratory WEIRD vs. less-WEIRD comparison found no meaningful sign that this reduction, or the effect's presence, was specific to the Western student samples the effect was first demonstrated in.
findings.source_title: Many Labs 2: Investigating Variation in Replicability Across Samples and Settings
findings.source_venue: Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science

findings.description: The same decision problem, described in terms of gains (e.g. 'saves 200 of 600 lives') versus an equivalent loss framing (e.g. '400 of 600 will die'), produced systematically different choices — people preferred the certain option when framed as a gain but the risky option when the identical outcome was framed as a loss. Demonstrated in both hypothetical and real monetary choices and in decisions about the loss of human lives (the 'Asian disease problem'), extending prospect theory's value function into a concrete, replicable demonstration of how a decision's presentation, not just its substance, shapes real choices.
findings.source_title: The Framing of Decisions and the Psychology of Choice

applications.title: Grammarly reframing 'skip' as 'skipping personalization'
applications.description: Grammarly's onboarding survey labels the option to bypass a question as 'skipping personalization' rather than a neutral 'skip' or 'next' -- reframing the same action to emphasize what the user would be giving up, intended to increase how many questions users actually complete.
applications.ethical_note: The reframing is honest in substance -- skipping a personalization question genuinely does mean less personalization, so nothing is fabricated -- but it's still a deliberate loss-framing choice designed to discourage an action the user might otherwise take freely. Graded mixed rather than user_beneficial since the goal is explicitly to change behavior via framing, not just inform.

applications.title: Resume-now.com deferring account creation until after resume work begins
applications.description: Resume-now.com lets visitors immediately pick a template and start customizing a resume before creating an account, framing the eventual signup request around content the user has already invested time in rather than asking upfront -- using the sunk time investment to frame registration as protecting existing work rather than a new cost.
applications.ethical_note: This isn't deceptive -- the user's work is genuinely real and genuinely at risk of being lost without an account -- but it does rely on a felt sunk-cost pressure to convert, rather than the user having decided upfront that an account is worth creating. Graded mixed to reflect that real pressure, distinct from a purely value-first pattern like the Nielsen Company reciprocity entry elsewhere in this corpus.
